docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Warning

This is project under development. Until version 0.3 is released, this repository will be unstable. Previous versions of the language are deprecated and not fully functioning.

H-hat is a rule system, compiler framework, and a statically typed, functional and distributed-system inspired, hybrid quantum-classical programming language family.

Targeted at software developers. This ecosystem requires no prior knowledge on quantum physics. For quantum technologies to become widely available, they must interoperate with existing software, and must be easier for software developers to reason about the quantum paradigm without a PhD in quantum information or quantum computing. Most of the features are intuitive, both classical and quantum can exist in the same code, and the quantum side is as easy to code as in the classical one.

Ships with Heather dialect. A simple but reasonable programming language, Heather aims to demonstrate the capabilities of the H-hat ecosystem. Check it out at the hhat-heather crate.

State-of-the-art software concepts. Latest software paradigms and cutting-edge features are presented for both classical and quantum sides, enabling a seamless coding experience, with smart compilation. The features and capabilities H-hat aims to accomplish and delivery are briefly described at the paper "Toward Declarative Platform-Independent Modeling of Hybrid Quantum--Classical Software".

Building quantum open-source software. Not only quantum software should advance, but we believe open-source is the backbone of world's most important software applications and tools. We are proudly supported by UnitaryFoundation.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
H-hat rule system defines how each dialect should behave in specific contexts. Below some of those rules are presented:

  • Classical and quantum entities must be able to coexist in the same program.
  • Quantum paradigm is a first-class entity just as its classical counterpart. It possesses quantum types, literals, constants, variables and functions that are denoted by the @ prefix.
  • No quantum physics properties such as qubits, quantum states, gates, circuits, pulses, Hamiltonians, or measurements are exposed to the user as language constructs. They are handled internally by the compiler, keeping the dialects platform-independent and problem-domain oriented.
  • Quantum functions must be declarative in nature to keep the quantum model abstracted away from platform-specific definitions. Quantum low-level languages and target backends will define how each primitive quantum function is interpreted.
  • Quantum data is lazily evaluated and linear, requiring a cast operator to realize it, to consume it and to drop it.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text: We coexist in the same world. So be nice to others as you expect others to be nice to you :)

docs.title: Contributing to H-hat
docs.text:
You can check the issues in the H-hat issue's page and try contributing on the issues with good first issue label. Depending on the programming language you are using, some formatting styles and checks are required. For instance:

  • Python:

    • Pull Request (PR) code should follow formatting from pre-commit configuration and pyproject.

  • Rust:

    • Besides from rust formatter and analyzer, cargo clippy, cargo check and cargo audit are recommended to run, because they are checked during GitHub Actions.

Additionally to code contribution, you are encourage to make part of discussions involving how H-hat can handle some language features or concepts. Reach us out at the Discord's #h-hat channel to learn more on how to contribute on that and also to chill and chat, if you feel like doing so.

docs.title: AI Contributions
docs.text: The rise of Generative AI brought many advancements for newcomers to start writing code, but also created concerning situations when incorporating AI-generated code to repositories. Regardless whether you choose to use the tool or not, the code you put in a PR is your responsibility. Make sure you checked it is doing what is intended to do, and does not introduce unnecessary complexity or bugs to the existing codebase. Simply AI prompted code will not be accepted. You are required to evaluate the intent of existing issue or PR, the existing codebase, and the code you are bringing up. Should your PR produce automated AI content (description and content) without support of your critical thinking, it will be closed.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Living document

This roadmap reflects current priorities and may change as development progresses. Items may be moved, reprioritized, or added.

Author input needed

The status of individual items below is approximate. The maintainers should confirm what is done, in progress, and planned, and add target milestones where useful.

docs.title: Short-term goals (current focus)
docs.text:
• Function implementation and built-in functions
  • CLI tooling for project management
  • Heather syntax and grammar finalization
  • Core type system (primitive types, structs, enums)
  • Frontend compilation pipeline (PEG parsing to HIR)
  • Cast system implementation
  • Meta-function implementation
  • Modifier implementation
  • Quantum program logic and accumulator
  • Initial quantum backend integration (OpenQASM v2)
  • LSP support for Heather
  • Documentation expansion

docs.title: Mid-term goals
docs.text:
• Documentation toolchain (auto-generated docs from code)
  • CLI distribution and packaging
  • Full Heather parsing and compilation
  • JIT compiler pipeline via Cranelift
  • Cast engine (reflective cast mechanism)
  • QPU device targeting (IBM hardware)
  • CPU architecture support (x86_64, aarch64)
  • Green threads and concurrency engine
  • Ownership, borrowing, and drop semantics
  • Meta-programming features
  • Sub-compiler communication protocol
  • Optimization passes (classical)
  • Quantum network backend (NetQASM/QNE)
  • User guides and tutorials

docs.title: Long-term vision
docs.text:
• AOT (ahead-of-time) compiler
  • Language bootstrapping (H-hat written in H-hat)
  • Online package registry
  • Dialect and library ecosystem
  • Formal verification integration
  • Proof assistant (Lean integration)
  • Advanced quantum optimization passes
  • Additional quantum backends (trapped ion, neutral atoms, photonics)
  • Distributed quantum computation support

docs.title: Version scheme
docs.text:
• 0.3.# — Rust implementation (stable development track)
  • 0.3-E# — Python implementation (experimental, now archived)

The first public release target is v0.3, covering the short-term goals above.

docs.text: Mind behind H-hat quantum programming language project.

docs.title: Inho
docs.text: Description in progress

docs.title: Roadmap for the first working version
docs.text: It is with satisfaction that I, Dooms, announce the roadmap for a first working version of H-hat. For legacy reasons, it will be starting as the version 0.3.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The H-hat development will be divided into two steps: Python based (step 1), and Rust based (step 2)
  • For everyone, the way to use the language is through the Rust-written interpreter/compiler (aka stable)
  • For those willing to test new features or even develop them, the Python-written interpreter/compiler is the way to go (aka experimental)
  • Heather is the default H-hat's dialect shipped with either Python or Rust interpreter/compiler
  • Version 0.3-E0 in Python to roll over by the beginning of next year, as well as initial development for 0.3.0 in Rust

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: So far, exploratory steps were taken mercilessly, scrapping, rewriting, fixing things without second thoughts. Now, things are getting more clear and solid, specifically on my proficiency at understanding what software requirements for the language development are needed, as well as improving the community interaction and exploring how to design a toolchain around it.

docs.title: Python and Rust
docs.text:
A common sense between me and Inho (mostly) is that, while the language is not bootstrappeable and there is a mismatch between people interested on quantum with programming language skills and good programming languages to build programming languages, there is going to be a two-step development cycle system for H-hat: step 1 is test it in Python, and step 2 is establish it in Rust.

In practice, it means that new features, new ideas, new concepts, and breaking changes will be first developed in Python. Why is that? Because most of the people with some knowledge and interest in quantum right now may be (only or mostly) familiar with Python, so we want to make sure their ideas and suggestions can be easily tested/added to the language so we can understand how things will work. Thus, for those willing to test new features or develop them, the Python-written interpreter/compiler is the way to go.

Once those features/changes are accepted to be incorporated into H-hat, the next step is followed; let's implement that in Rust. It means that stable, (much more) performant and reliant version of the language will be written in Rust. For everyone, this will be the way to use the language: through the Rust-written interpreter/compiler. But, why Rust? you may ask. Simple reason I can find is: I would rather write it in Rust than in any other language that can offer some performance due to their systems programming capabilities and compiled nature. And since Rust seems to be a good language to do most of the work needed here and people are willing to learn it, it seems compelling to pursue this PATH.

docs.title: Versioning scheme
docs.text:
Now, regarding the versioning. Python code version will be defined as the experimental side of things, so its versioning scheme is as follows: <MAJOR>.<MINOR>-E<PATCH> (example: 0.3-E1 ), while Rust code version will be defined as the stable side and thus having the versioning scheme as: <MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH> (example: 0.3.4).

The distinction between both is to make it clear what their purposes are for, so there is no confusion which one to download or build, for instance. Also, it shows that the patch version from Python's has no relation to the patch version of Rust's, because they may have independent cycles and independent bugs/fixes.

The only thing they share is the core concepts to be leverage from one to the other. It means that a version 0.3-Ex in Python code version should present the same language features as the one in version 0.3.y in Rust (where x and y are unrelated to each other). It also means that Python code version will always be ahead of Rust's. Once 0.3-Ex is approved, the pipeline will move towards implementing the features described on it to the Rust code version. It alone will have the traditional scope, as 0.3.0-beta for beta versions and 0.3.0 once it is officially released, for instance. Regarding release candidate (e.g. 0.3.0-rc), it still is not clear, but let's see how it goes. At that point, Python code version must start developing at the version 0.4-Ex.

I also plan to have a 0.3-STABLE tag to direct to the latest, most stable version (in Rust). I particularly am not a fan of having version x.y.z overall, because you never know which z is the latest or more stable one. This will align better with some ideas I have for the future of the language as well. But I will discuss it in a future post.

docs.title: Dialects
docs.text:
One important aspect of H-hat is to be a rule system with core concepts to be followed, rather than a strict syntax, semantics and compilation implementation. The reason is that throughout the years presenting H-hat to people from various backgrounds, I noticed a pattern: people always want to have something familiar to look for; thus, I always had the "why not having the syntax as ?". I realized that nobody was happy with any syntax I would ever try to present to appease their tastes. So instead, I decided to define the rules in which H-hat is composed on and write dialects on top of it to demonstrate the features I want to present.

In the long term, I envision some interoperability between dialects happening, so people could write their own dialect with their favorite syntax/semantics and easily integrate with existing code or be easily integrated with future code in other dialects.

For now, Heather is the current dialect that ships with the language (Python and Rust code versions will have it). Its main point is to manifest H-hat capabilities, so we can build things and understand how to do better in the next version.

docs.title: Content of version 0.3
docs.text:
• Types definitions: single, struct, enum
  • Heather dialect
  • Classical and quantum data types and functions constructs
  • Built-in data types:
  • bool
  • u32
  • u64
  • i32

  • f32
  • f64
  • str
  • hashmap
  • @bool
  • @u2
  • @u3

  • Built-in functions:
  • basic IO features on: keyboard input and binary file reading, terminal printing and binary file writing

docs.title: Version 0.3 release roadmap
docs.text:
• Python, experimental version (0.3-Ex)
  • September and October: built-in functions feature, openqasmv2 and cast system
  • October and November: cast system, qiskit and modifier feature
  • November and December: netqasm, modifier and meta module features
  • January and February: netsquid, distributed features

Rust version will follow through shortly.

docs.title: Final remarks
docs.text:
Exciting months ahead and looking forward to knowing what you think about it! You can reach us out at the Unitary Foundation's Discord server (linked at README.md file) #h-hat channel.

See you around :))

docs.title: Follow up on the roadmap for version 0.3
docs.text:
As discussed previously, I will give a little bit more information on the actual roadmap.

Considering I am focusing on studying, designing and writing code for H-hat in the coming weeks/months with part-time dedication and eventually some people will be helping here and there, the goals and timelines are:

docs.title: Codebase
docs.text:
[!NOTE]

The order of the items does not reflect their priority or implementation order.

docs.title: Finish minimal function implementation capabilities
docs.text:
How to invoke built-in, in-code or external (library/package) functions. In principle, they should use the same principles behind. In the case of built-in ones, a special space of the BaseIRInstr class so it can also follow the same workflow, aka be called through resolve method to address the correct function.

Considering Heather dialect uses function overloading, it will try to find the correct function through the combination of arguments types provided and the given function name. However, it cannot figure out the function output type, so a same function same with same number and types of arguments must not have different definitions with different outputs.

docs.title: Add minimal built-in functions (dialect or core?)
docs.text:
A very specific set of built-in functions will be added at this moment. Hopefully I can get enough feedback to choose the best ones for the first working version. So your feedback matters here (or anywhere where you can find me, really)!

It is still uncertain whether it should be: (1) a core feature or a dialect-specific feature, (3) available by default or need to do some function importing.

docs.title: Implement cast system
docs.text: Cast system is a core feature of H-hat, and it has been tried a few times so far, with different outcomes from each iteration. I will write more about it in a separated post, but so far it suffices to say that this feature contains the heart of all I think is important to provide the proper level of high abstraction from programmers using quantum resources.

docs.title: Refactor/reimplement OpenQASMv2 code logic and structure
docs.text: This needs to be rethought... again. This part always seems easy and lazy to do, but always prove hard to be good enough to be extensible for all the optimizations and passes available by Qiskit ecosystem or some other custom-made features, and at the same time have a robust enough base API to be used by it or any other low level language (such as NetQASM). I keep postponing improving this part... maybe other things are more priority or interesting.

docs.title: Finish cast system implementation (structure and logic)
docs.text: Nothing much to say here. Cast system is a delicate structure that interfaces quantum types with classical ones while performing all the execution requests, checks and casting type part for the quantum programs. It may take longer, but I hope that I have enough experience and material from previous iterations to finalize it by October (at most beginning of November?).

docs.title: Finish working on OpenQASMv2 base code
docs.text: I may drag this throughout October, but be nice (or do it for me 👼 ).

docs.title: Refactor/reimplement Qiskit code logic and structure for target backends (no optimizations, extra passes, etc. yet)
docs.text: This part is less traumatic than the OpenQASMv2 part (can't even start thinking of OpenQASMv3 yet), but it needs to have a good base API to handle not only Qiskit but also any other target backend infrastructure, such as NetQASM/SquidASM/AWSBraket/etc. So in the end, doing Qiskit will help shape the base API for it (and of course implement it throughout the process) and future backends.

docs.title: Implement modifier feature
docs.text:
Modifier is a nice (I hope) feature I have been thinking that may bring some power to the programmer and also clarity on the code. It basically enables to modify the behavior, property or add extra properties to some instance, should it be a variable or a function, for example. The syntax is something<mdfr-arg1=mdfr-value1 mdfr-arg2=mdfr-value2>, where the <> brackets defines the scope of the modifier for a given instance (something in this case). A few simple examples:

  • some-var<&> means the reference of some-var, or &some_var in some other languages, like Rust or C
  • @some-var<shots=3000> means it will use 3000 shots for this quantum variable execution on the backend, regardless the default configuration is

In most cases, the modifier argument needs a argument name and a value. In specific unequivocal cases, a symbol alone can be used (as is the case of the reference &). It may stack modifiers and their order must not matter, unless they are used in different moments throughout the code. In the later case, the current modifier overwrites any repeated modifier argument, but must use all previous ones.

Maybe having a tag in the modifier stating "use it once" should be a good idea, so that the modifier will only work at that specific moment and not after.

docs.title: More modifier
docs.text: Hopefully it will be done by November.

docs.title: Meta module feature
docs.text: Something that bothers me a lot in Python is the hacky way to do dynamic imports. So I thought "why not trying to do something better, like creating a meta module with a template so other modules can use it and define their expected functions and behaviors?". Seemed a good idea, so I am going to implement it. Still unsure whether it makes sense to be implemented at this point, but I see potential and need for it.

docs.title: NetQASM implementation
docs.text:
It is not the first implementation, but will be the first successful working one. On the previous ones, I spent too much time fighting with divergent approaches and could never make up my mind on which one to use. In the end, I had to focus on other things, and it was put aside to freeze. It will basically take the same ideas from OpenQASMv2 successful implementation and, using the base API, should be no more than writing down the NetQASM-specific instructions.

Previously, I was stuck because NetQASM uses a very thoughtful approach to have internal memory for classical and quantum data inside its routines. It was very nice for NetQASM, but very hard to access it smoothly from the outside to read or write its content. I ended up lost in their code logic and couldn't find a neat solution at that time without changing H-hat internals. Result: I had to change H-hat internals to account for that. So I decided to create a memory manager for quantum programs that basically handles classical and quantum memory, qubits, scopes and other relevant resources. It is still not extensible, so if in the future some other low level language requires other kinds of features, I may need to rethink... again.

docs.title: December
docs.text: December will be full of wrapping up previous tasks.

docs.title: NetSquid/SquidASM
docs.text: Then, it comes to the time of implementing NetSquid/SquidASM (maybe Simulaqron?) backend. I just think that having at least one "standalone" and one quantum networks backends would make sense to test, try and develop relevant features that the language want the programmer to benefit from and also to learn how to create them.

docs.title: Distributed features
docs.text: Besides the quantum networks backend, H-hat needs to have some support that can show such capabilities even if just on simulators. So having distributed features is very important, but maybe not detrimental for the release of version 0.3. Let's see how it works out.

docs.title: Release!(?)
docs.text: At this point, it should be able to be good enough to at least be tested. Hopefully, kind people will join to help feedback, guide and improve the features, language and its ecosystem, and maybe even be part of the community!

docs.title: February
docs.text: I expect February be a January++.

docs.title: Conferences
docs.text:
Besides the code development side, some interesting conferences are right in the horizon and I think they cannot be missed (again). I missed a few ones this year due to work and personal reasons, for instance, the 2nd Workshop on Quantum Software 2025 in Seoul (https://pldi25.sigplan.org/home/wqs-2025) and the 7th International Workshop on Quantum Compilation in Helsinki (https://quantum-compilers.github.io/iwqc25/). So now, there are a few opportunities coming up due this year:

  • Munich Quantum Software Forum 2025 (https://www.cda.cit.tum.de/research/quantum/mqsf/); H-hat was accepted and is attending! preparations in progress
  • Seventh International Workshop on Quantum Software Engineering (Q-SE 2026) (https://conf.researchr.org/home/icse-2026/q-se-2026); checking viability
  • International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC 2026) (https://www.ieee-qcnc.org/2026/); draft in progress

docs.title: On the stable version part
docs.text:
Depending on how things evolve people-wise, code-wise, time-wise, opportunities-wise, it may be possible to resume the Rust side, making the actual JIT compiler for the stable version. And that is another exciting challenge and project on its own that I have been studying and testing a few things (with less frequency). Using Pliron, Cranelift or Melior framework?

I have been in touch with Pliron's creator and collaborators, and it has been a very interesting experience so far to learn about it. Still unsure how practical it can be to use on its current state for H-hat current needs, but definitely I want to test it in practice. Cranelift is another one that caught my attention, especially because its JIT compiler-driven features already in place.

If that depends only on me, I will try to use whatever uses less C++ for now.

docs.title: Final remarks
docs.text:
I hope this post can bring some light on what is in progress and what is planned for the coming months. Hopefully more people can join the effort! Feedback, reviews, discussions, beta testing, coding, designing, emotional support. Anything helps!

Well, that is it. Until the next post.

docs.title: On design choices and relevance
docs.text:
For the last several months that I have been working on the working version 0.3 I had a vision that people engaging in the process and helping shape and build the language would be a net positive and necessary step towards a relevant tool and its further applications.

By now I realized that it was not the case. People want something done, ready to play or to use. They want to test and see what it is capable of doing, rather than contributing to it. And that ultimately makes sense.

I spent many months trying to engage people to build together in-progress concepts, ideas and design plans, at the same time trying to implement a language in Python so they could also participate in the process. Experience shows that: (1) it is very difficult to provide useful features coming from a higher abstraction level language when building another language on it; (2) it is very hard to make people engaged without something barely concrete and working so they can visualize what they are into; (3) some decisions are better off providing at first and collecting feedbacks and changing as people experiment with the language and its approach.

After fighting unnecessary abstractions and distractions in Python, I decided to move completely and definitely to Rust. The idea is to speed up the process and provide a more stable and faster experience for the programmer while improving the code quality, code consistency and ease of code low level parts for the language development. I now know most people are waiting to use it instead of joining in design decisions, paradigm discussions and definitions, and so on.

Therefore delay is happening for the release, but it gives quality for everyone. UnitaryDESIGN is happening soon (Feb 16th-27th, 2026), which will help improving documentation and some aesthetics and cosmetics aspects of the project.

I see more and more some convergence on what I am trying to accomplish with the language out there, but it is still not enough. I still believe we need to provide better vision, care and thoughtful choices especially now, for the programmers of current and the generations to come, as well bring a more balanced society.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A glossary is available containing the list of acronyms and terminologies used throughout this documentation. It covers basic terms such as QPU, IR, and compiler pass. You can find it at the Glossary page. The page is filled dynamically, so new entries are added from time to time.

docs.title: Rule system
docs.text: The rule system is used to define expected behaviors for the H-hat compliant compilers. You can find more information at the Rule system page.

docs.title: Heather dialect
docs.text: Heather is a programming language shipped with H-hat that aims at providing the minimal useful features a H-hat language should have while being compliant with the rule system. You can find more find more about at Heather dialect page.

docs.title: Dialects
docs.text: Dialects are programming languages that share the H-hat infrastructure and comply with the rule system. Find more about them at the Dialects page.

docs.title: Compiler framework
docs.text: The compiler framework provides means for dialect builders and their compilers to express internal H-hat features without having to write them from scratch. It provides standardization on compilation passes, diagnostics and future interoperability between dialects. You can find more at the Compiler framework page.

docs.title: Toolchain framework
docs.text: H-hat has a toolchain framework that enables dialect builders to import features without the need to write them from scratch. Those tools include the CLI that consists mainly of the project creation and management. More information at Toolchain framework page.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: In this page you can find the table of contents for acronyms, its meanings and descriptions, and terminologies and their meanings/descriptions. The entries are in alphabetical order. More entries are being added from time to time.

docs.title: Acronyms
docs.text: Acronym Meaning Description CLI command line interface A user interface through typing commands on the terminal. HIR high-level IR A high-level IR that usually contains more information about the original source code. Useful for debugging early stages of the copmilation pass, for instance to catch up parsing errors. IR intermediate representation A code user internally by the compiler that represents the source code. MIR mid-level IR A mid-level IR that is usually stripped off of the original source code. It is closer to the machine code and contains more instructions from the internal compiler logic, internal checks, diagnostics. Q3L quantum low-level language A quantum language with quantum physics constructs, such as qubits, gates or Hamiltonians/pulses, quantum circuit, etc., that can be used by quantum backends for executing quantum programs. Examples are OpenQASM v2, OpenQASM v3, NetQASM, cQASM. QPU quantum processing unit A quantum mechanics-based hardware that uses qubits as the processing units.

docs.title: Terminologies
docs.text: Terminology Meaning/Description Compiler pass A stage of compilation in which some specific processing, transformation, optimization, or lowering happens. Quantum backend A target device or simulator that can be used to execute quantum programs.

docs.title: H-hat dialects
docs.text:
H-hat language family enables dialects to be built following strict rules to keep compliance with its rule system, and to provide a consistent experience for users programming in H-hat.

H-hat ecosystem ships with Heather, a simple but reasonable programming language. It has all the minimum features required by H-hat rule system and compiler framework with a consistent grammar to improve the ease of coding.

You can also build your own dialect.

docs.title: Build your own H-hat dialect
docs.text:
Info

This section is a work in progress.

Dialects are programming languages that follow some common rules or behaviors, usually according to the main programming language's directive.

H-hat is not a programming language per se; it instead defines, designs and creates the structure, logic and frameworks in which programming languages can utilize to be compliant with H-hat principles.

More information on how to get started with dialect creation will follow in this page.

docs.title: Heather
docs.text:
Heather is the reference programming language shipped with H-hat. It is named after a plant1 and a song2.

The language is being developed to present all the concepts H-hat aims to accomplish: high-level abstraction language, rule system for strong compliance on quantum rules and quantum physics-respecting constraints, and to present a quantum software engineering side closer to the classical one.

It has some basic features, as well simple syntax; grammar strict structure and almost no ambiguity (if any) highlights Heather capabilities, promoting code that is easy to write, read, and reason about.

You can find the following under the sub-pages:

  • Syntax page
  • Grammar page

docs.title: Language features
docs.text:
• Statically typed
  • Ownership, borrowing and drop
  • No garbage collector
  • JIT compiler by Cranelift
  • Call-oriented functions and operators

  1. Scientific name: Calluna vulgaris, a small flowering shrub. ↩

  2. Billy Cobham's Crosswinds album, second track of side two. ↩

docs.title: Heather grammar
docs.text:
Info

Grammar shortcuts: behavioral, types, constants, proofs.

Common grammar features:

  • Single line comments: // <comment>
  • Multiline comments: /- <comment block> -/
  • Whitespaces: space , tab \t, new line \n, comma ,, and semi-colon ;

docs.title: Behavioral
docs.text:
The behavioral grammar can be found at:

program                     = imports* group_fns* main? EOF
imports                     = "use" "(" ( type_import | fn_import | metafn_import | modifier_import | supertype_import | const_import )+ ")"
type_import                 = "type" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
fn_import                   = "fn" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
metafn_import               = "metafn" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
modifier_import             = "modifier" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
supertype_import            = "super-type" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
const_import                = "const" ":" ( single_import | many_imports )
single_import               = composite_id_with_closure | full_id
many_imports                = "[" single_import+ "]"
composite_id_with_closure   = full_id "." "{" ( composite_id_with_closure | full_id )+ "}"
full_id                     = simple_id ( "." ( int_t | simple_id ) )* modifier?
simple_id                   = r"(\?)?(\@)?[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9\-_]*"
modifier                    = "<" ( ( ref | pointer | variadic | callargs | simple_id ) modifier?)+ ">"
ref                         = "&"
pointer                     = "*"
variadic                    = "..."
callargs                    = simple_id "=" valonly
valonly                     = array | literal | full_id
array                       = "[" ( array | literal | full_id )* "]"
literal                     = (bool_t | float_t | int_t | str_t ) modifier?
bool_t                      = r"(\@)?(true|false)"
int_t                       = r"(\@)?(-)?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)"
float_t                     = r"(\@)?(-)?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\.[0-9]+"
str_t                       = "\"" ( str_char | "{" simple_id "}" )* "\""
str_char                    = r"[^\"\\{}\n]" | r"\\."
main                        = "main" body
body                        = "{" ( declareassign | declareassign_ds | declare | assign | assign_ds | expr )* "}"
declareassign               = simple_id modifier? ":" type_id "=" expr
declareassign_ds            = simple_id modifier? ":" type_id "=" "." "{" ( assign+ | expr+ ) "}"
declare                     = simple_id modifier? ":" type_id
assign                      = full_id "=" expr
assign_ds                   = full_id "." "{" ( assign+ | expr+ ) "}"
expr                        = cast | literal | array | access | call_optn | call_optbdn | call_bdn | call | full_id
cast                        = ( access | call | literal | full_id ) "*" modifier? type_id
access                      = callable member+
callable                    = call_optn | call_optbdn | call_bdn | call
member                      = "." ( simple_id | int_t | ( "(" args* ")" ) )
call_optn                   = full_id "(" option+ ")"
call_optbdn                 = full_id "(" args* ")" "{" option+ "}" modifier?
call_bdn                    = full_id "(" args* ")" fn_body modifier?
option                      = expr ":" ( fn_return | fn_body )
call                        = full_id "(" args* ")" modifier?
args                        = ( cast | literal | array | access | call | valonly )
group_fns                   = fn_def | metafn_def | modifier_def | supertype_def
fn_def                      = "fn" simple_id fn_args type_id? fn_body
fn_args                     = "(" argtype* ")"
argtype                     = simple_id modifier? ":" type_id
type_id                     = ( "[" full_id "]" ) | full_id
fn_body                     = "{" ( fn_return | declareassign | declareassign_ds | declare | assign | assign_ds | expr )* "}"
fn_return                   = "::" expr
metafn_def                  = "metafn" simple_id fn_args type_id? metafn_body
metafn_body                 = "{" ( fn_return | declareassign | declareassign_ds | declare | assign_ds | assign | option | expr )* "}"
modifier_def                = "modifier" ( simple_id | pointer | ref | variadic ) modifier_args type_id modifier_body
modifier_args               = "(" "self" argtype* ")"
modifier_body               = "{" modifier_item+ "}"
modifier_item               = modifier_directive ":" ( fn_body | fn_return | expr )
modifier_directive          = "#ct_init" | "#rt_init" | "#ct_read" | "#rt_read" | "#ct_write" | "#rt_write" | "#ct_drop" | "#rt_drop"
supertype_def               = "super-type" simple_id supertype_body
supertype_body              = "{" full_id* "}"

docs.title: Heather syntax
docs.text:
Info

Work in progress.

How a "hello world" looks like in Heather (main.hat):

main { print("hello world") }

Heather has no need for ; to separate between statements or , to separate between items. , \t, \n, ; and , are all treated as whitespaces and are ignored. You may use them if you prefer though. Because of Heather's regular syntax, statements and expressions can be organized in what fits better the programmer's or a particular project style. We expect that it can provide some freedom for people to experiment and define what works better for a particular situation, rather than enforcing that without a real reason. Comments are: // comment goes here for line comments, and /* comment body goes inside here */ for multiline comments.

docs.title: 1. Constants
docs.text:
Constants are defined inside consts.hat files. They have the following syntax:

const <name>:<type> = <value>

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
math/consts.hat:

const pi32:f32 = 3.14159265
const pi64:f64 = 3.141592653589793

io/consts.hat:

const localhost:str = "localhost"

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
You can import constants in functions kinds and other constants files.

For single imports:

use(const:math.pi)

For multiple imports:

use(
    const:math.e
    const:math.phi
)

For multiple imports inside a single const:

use(
    const:[
      math.{pi e phi}
      io.localhost
    ]
)

docs.title: 2. Types
docs.text: Types are defined inside custom files located on src/hat_types/ path. There are basically two types of user types: structs and enums. A quantum type can contain classical types as its members/named values, but the opposite is not valid.

docs.title: Structs
docs.text: Definition: a composite data structure, holding a collection of members (or fields) that may have different data types.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: type <name> { <member>:<type> ... }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining struct type:

type point { x:i32 y:i32 }

Using struct type:

// assigning to variable p while declaring it
p:point =.{x=34 y=43}

// assigning to variable already declared
p2:point
p2.{x=15 y=51}

// (re)assigning to individual members
p3<mut>:point
p3.{x=143 y=331}
p3.y=341

// calling it
print(p.x)

Importing:

// single import
use(type:math.geometry.point)

// multiple imports:
use(
    type:math.geometry.point3d
    type:math.trigonometry.rad
)

// multiple imports, single call:
use(
    type:[
      math.{
        geometry.{point point3d} 
        trigonometry.rad
      }
      status.status_t
    ]
)

docs.title: Enums
docs.text: Definition: a tagged union (or enumerated) data structure that can contain a collection of named values, those being simple identifiers or structs, but only one can be in use at any one time. By convention, identifiers are all caps.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: type <name> { <enumerator?> <struct?> ... }

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
Defining enum type:

type status_t { ON OFF }

type result_t {
    data{
        value:sample_t
    }
    NONE
}

Using enum type:

// declaring and assigning on a variable
status:status_t = status_t.ON
res:result_t = result_t.data.value=...
res2:result_t = result_t.NONE

// assigning on a declared variable
status2:status_t
status2 = status_t.ON

// calling it
print(status_t.OFF)
print(status)

docs.title: Syntax:
docs.text:
fn <name> (<args?>) <type?> { <body?> }

Return has a special syntax sugar: :: prefixed on an expression.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining a type:

fn sum(a:i64 b:i64) i64 { ::add(a b) }

fn print-gt(a:u64 b:u64) {
    if(
      gt(a b): print(a)
      true: print(b)
    )
}

docs.title: 4. Meta-funcions
docs.text: Definition: a function that defines the code behavior assigned to it. There are three kinds of meta-functions: option (or cases), body (or blocks), and option-body (or case-blocks). They have the types associated with them as optn_t, bdn_t and optbdn_t respectively.

docs.title: Syntax:
docs.text: metafn <name> (args) <type?> { <body> }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
if meta-function (option type):

Defining:

metafn if(options:[opt-body_t]) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

if(gt(a b):a true:b)

pipe meta-function (body type):

Defining:

metafn pipe(args:[expr_t] body:ir_t) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

pipe(var) { double print }  // applies double on var and then print on double's result

match meta-function (option-body type):

Defining:

metafn match(arg:[expr_t] options:[opt-body_t]) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

match(status) {
  status_t.ON:print("on!")
  status_t.OFF:print("off!")
}

docs.title: 5. Modifiers
docs.text: Definition: a function that can change the semantics and properties of its holder.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
modifier <name> (self <arg?>) <type> { <body> }

the <type> must be the same of self.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
& (reference) modifier

modifier &(self) u32 { ... }  // for u32 type
modifier &(self) [u32] { ... }  // for array of u32 type
modifier &(self) status_t { ... }  // for status_t type

// setting a variable `var` of type "reference of status_t"
var:status_t<&>

docs.title: 6. Cast
docs.text: Definition: a type of reflective function and semantics that convert one data into another type. If data is eagerly evaluated (strict), it should convert to target type calling a given function with given cast name and the appropriate argument types signature. If data is lazily evaluated (lazy), it will evoke its evaluation and then the result value to be cast into the target type. It has a syntax sugar * when called, as in: data * type, meaning "cast data into type".

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: fn cast (data:<type> to:<type>) <to type> { <body> }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Casting strict data:

v1:u32 = 42
// now v1 data is cast into u64 and stored in v2
v2:u64 = v1 * u64

Casting lazy data:

@q:@bell_t =.{@s=@false @t=@false}
@sync(@q)
// evaluate lazy data from @q and convert
//   its result as hashmap with key u64 
//   and value bool, storing at res
res:hashmap<%u64 %bool> = @q * hashmap<%u64 %bool>

docs.title: Rule system
docs.text:
Info

Section in progress. More information to be added.

the H-hat rule system governs the specification of the dialects and their well-formedness rules, in which all languages must adhere to be part of the language family. Concretely, the rules are the following:

Classical and quantum entities must be able to coexist in the same program. Quantum paradigm is a first-class entity just as its classical counterpart. It possesses quantum types, literals, constants, variables and functions that are denoted by the @ prefix.

Quantum data must be lazily evaluated and linear, requiring a cast operator to realize it, to consume it and to drop it.

Reflective cast is an operator that takes one data and one type as arguments. If the data is quantum and type is classical, it triggers the realization of the accumulated instructions inside the quantum data, their emission as a Q3L and execution (with measurements) in a target backend, with subsequent sampling outcome being translated into the target classical type according to some rules described in Section 5. The classical type can be a wildcard value when all that quantum data’s fields have been previously cast.

No quantum physics properties such as qubits, quantum states, gates, circuits, pulses, Hamiltonians or measurement are exposed to the user as language constructs. They are handled internally by the compiler, keeping the dialects platform-independent.

Quantum functions must be declarative in nature to keep the quantum model abstracted away from platform-specific definitions. Quantum low-level languages and target backends will define how each primitive quantum function is interpreted. Quantum functions may have classical arguments, and must be accumulated when applied to quantum data. The rule system must fix each primitive’s signature and intended effect on the data model. A reference semantics is future work, with backends implementing against it.

Artefact kinds are the definitional artefacts (types, constants, behavioral definitions) and the companion artefacts (documentation and proofs) which are first-class entities and live in their own specific locations, with specific but dialect-coherent grammars. Compiler passes may trigger them through different model-driven processes.

Companion artefacts are specifically part of the rule system’s model-driven process, being a project’s mandatory artefacts invoked through the toolchain during flagged building and release steps.

docs.title: What is H-hat
docs.text:
H-hat is a rule system, compiler framework, and a statically typed, functional and distributed-system inspired, hybrid quantum-classical programming language family. As an ecosystem, H-hat provides all the infrastructure for dialect builders so dialects comply with the high-level abstraction paradigm and rule system. Users benefit from using a higher-level abstraction language with well-formedness principles and a unified toolchain.

Writing programs with quantum code is as natural as classical code.

Quantum and classical code may coexist in the same program. Quantum paradigm contains quantum types, quantum literals, quantum variables and quantum functions.

docs.title: Why H-hat
docs.text:
H-hat is intended to be used for designing problem-domain programs. Therefore:

  • H-hat abstracts away the physics from the user
  • Focus on the problem domain instead of physical constraints

A new layer of abstraction unveils new possibilities to think and write about problems. That is the core of H-hat ecosystem. Just like Fortran revolutionalized as the first compiled programming language, H-hat hopes that having the capability to think of the problem and not the physics will enable a new wave of development and creativity.

docs.title: How to use H-hat
docs.text: To use H-hat is necessary to use a programming language that implements H-hat. Luckily H-hat ships with Heather, a reference dialect. You can find it at the Heather dialect page.

docs.title: Version 0.3 (2026-2027)
docs.text:
Info

This roadmap page covers what is expected for the version 0.3 release. A more long-term roadmap will be available in the future.

H-hat version 0.3 is expected to bring the first fully working ecosystem, with Heather as a reference language. The following is an overview of the features to be available:

  • Rule system's rules for quantum logic and enforcing constraints
  • Rule system macros to be used in the dialect compiler building
  • Basic compiler logic on data (ownership, borrowing, drop checks)
  • Quantum low-level languages (Q3L) interfaces and quantum backends
  • Heather compiler passes (source to IR, IR to Cranelift, Cranelift's JIT, IR to Q3L, Q3L to quantum backend)
  • Basic typed message passing logic
  • Reflective cast mechanism
  • Minimal compiler diagnostics
  • Minimal CLI and toolchain features for project management

Below you can find features by category. The items are not necessarily presented in order of priority or logic.

docs.title: Rule system
docs.text:
• Rules for quantum data, logic and its behavior (creation, ownership, borrowing, drop, lazy data behavior and realization)
  • Procedural macros and macros for incorporating rules into dialect's host compiler
  • Rules checks on dialect's host compiler
  • Rules internal validation

docs.title: Compiler framework
docs.text:
• Compiler features for including the rule system on dialect's host compiler
  • Compiler features for including data lifetime cycle (creation, ownership, borrowing, dropping)
  • Compiler features for including the typed message passing
  • Typed message passing mechanism
  • Compiler passes for rules checks
  • Compiler checks and diagnostics for users' code
  • Reflective cast mechanism (realization of lazy quantum data)
  • Q3L

docs.title: Toolchain framework
docs.text: • CLI for project management (project creation, files creation, project update, project build, project execution)

docs.title: Heather dialect
docs.text:
• Compiler pass from source code to high-level interemediate representation (HIR)
  • Compiler pass from HIR to mid-level intermediate representation (MIR)
  • Compiler pass from MIR to Cranelift's CLIF and MIR to Q3L
  • Compiler pass from CLIF to machine code and execution
  • Compiler pass from Q3L to quantum backend, execution and output retrieval
  • Typed message passing mechanism
